name: Cedar Green
lede: Cedar green is a sixteenth-century painter's name for a copper-mineral green, and today a dull, deep green on color charts.

sections.title: A green with a tree's name
sections.body:
Coles reports that chrysocolla, a copper mineral, has been used as a green pigment since antiquity; it turns up at Kizil in Turkistan and in Egyptian tombs of the Twelfth Dynasty [1]. In oil it turns very translucent because its tinting strength is low [1]. It worked best in egg tempera and especially watercolor, and in the 16th century that use was called cedar green [1].

Our books say nothing more about the name, and who coined it is undocumented. The dull green on this page comes from later color lists: ISCC-NBS (1955), Ridgway (1912) and Maerz & Paul (1930) all carry the name [3]. We cannot show that this swatch matches the sixteenth-century pigment, so treat it as a modern reading of the word. Its neighbors are [[olive-green]], [[sage-green]] and [[dark-green]] and, among pigment greens, [[hooker-s-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Cedar green is common in our archive: it appears in 645 of 23,781 paintings, more than 78 per cent of the named colors manage [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 73 of 1,674 paintings, 2.8 times the museums' baseline [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test.

origin.named_after: not documented in our books (Coles gives the name only for the chrysocolla pigment)
origin.first_recorded: 16th century, as a watercolor and tempera pigment name

Why is chrysocolla translucent in oil?

openers: In oil, a copper-mineral green can turn glass-clear; painters kept it for watercolor and tempera.
